newsitem.title: UK: Yeast protein offers slight hope for mad cow cure.
newsitem.headline: Yeast protein offers slight hope for mad cow cure.

text.p: U.S. researchers have found a yeast protein that offers a distant, but real, hope for a cure for mad cow disease and its deadly human equivalent, New Scientist magazine reported on Thursday.
They said the yeast protein acted just like the rogue "prion" believed to be behind bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE or mad cow disease) and the human Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD).

Susan Lindquist and colleagues at the University of Chicago told a meeting of the American Society for Microbiology in Miami Beach that the yeast protein had a "chaperone" protein that made it behave normally.

BSE and CJD are called prion diseases because large numbers of normal brain proteins known as prions take on an abnormal folded form. They seem to be able to cause other prions to fold, but scientists do not yet understand how.
Lindquist's group studied what seemed to be an equivalent protein in yeast, known as Sup35. It, too, seemed to fold up and make other proteins fold too.
The researchers said the aggregations looked a lot like the "plaques" found in the brains of BSE and CJD victims, but another protein, known as HSP-104, could make Sup35 flip back to its normal form.

The next step was to see if the prion protein had a similar chaperone. "If you could tweak (production of the) chaperone a fewfold, it could have a huge impact on the disease symptoms," Lindquist was quoted as saying. But, she added: "It's a hope, that's all."
Only about one person in a million has contracted CJD but it is always fatal. Finding a cure has become more urgent since a possible link was found between BSE and a new form of CJD.
